claim: Human translation initiation factor eIF3 interacts with select immune system related mRNAs including those encoding the T cell receptor (TCR) subunits TCRA and TCRB.
source: Here, we show human translation initiation factor eIF3 interacts with select immune system related mRNAs including those encoding the T cell receptor (TCR) subunits TCRA and TCRB.
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP experimental data showing eIF3 crosslinking to TCRA and TCRB mRNAs in activated Jurkat cells (Figure 1E).

claim: Binding of eIF3 to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-untranslated regions (3'-UTRs) depends on CD28 coreceptor signaling.
source: Binding of eIF3 to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-untranslated regions (3'-UTRs) depends on CD28 coreceptor signaling and regulates a burst in TCR translation required for robust T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that anti-CD28 stimulation alone was sufficient to cause a transient burst in translation in nanoluciferase reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs (Figure 4).

claim: eIF3 binding to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs regulates a burst in TCR translation required for robust T cell activation.
source: Binding of eIF3 to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-untranslated regions (3'-UTRs) depends on CD28 coreceptor signaling and regulates a burst in TCR translation required for robust T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by data showing deletion of eIF3 PAR-CLIP sites in TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs eliminated the burst in TCR translation and impaired T cell activation markers (Figure 5).

claim: Use of the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs to control expression of an anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) improves the ability of CAR-T cells to kill tumor cells in vitro.
source: Use of the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs to control expression of an anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) improves the ability of CAR-T cells to kill tumor cells in vitro.
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing CAR T cells expressing the CAR using either the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR showed more robust killing of tumor cell lines (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Translation initiation serves as a key gatekeeper of protein synthesis in eukaryotes and requires the action of eukaryotic initiation factor 3 (eIF3).
source: Translation initiation serves as a key gatekeeper of protein synthesis in eukaryotes and requires the action of eukaryotic initiation factor 3 (eIF3) (Hernández et al., 2020; Pelletier and Sonenberg, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on translation initiation.

claim: In humans, eIF3 is a 13-subunit protein complex that coordinates the cellular machinery in positioning ribosomes at the mRNA start codon.
source: In humans, eIF3 is a 13-subunit protein complex that coordinates the cellular machinery in positioning ribosomes at the mRNA start codon.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of eIF3 structure and function.

claim: eIF3 serves specialized roles in cellular translation by recognizing specific RNA structures in the 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTRs) of target mRNAs.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate eIF3 also serves specialized roles in cellular translation, by recognizing specific RNA structures in the 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTRs) of target mRNAs (Lee et al., 2015), binding the 7-methyl-guanosine (m7G) cap (Lamper et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2016) or through interactions with N-6-methyl-adenosine (m6A) post-transcriptional modifications in mRNAs (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating these specialized roles.

claim: eIF3 can bind the 7-methyl-guanosine (m7G) cap.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate eIF3 also serves specialized roles in cellular translation, by recognizing specific RNA structures in the 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTRs) of target mRNAs (Lee et al., 2015), binding the 7-methyl-guanosine (m7G) cap (Lamper et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2016) or through interactions with N-6-methyl-adenosine (m6A) post-transcriptional modifications in mRNAs (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing eIF3 cap-binding activity.

claim: eIF3 interacts with N-6-methyl-adenosine (m6A) post-transcriptional modifications in mRNAs.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate eIF3 also serves specialized roles in cellular translation, by recognizing specific RNA structures in the 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTRs) of target mRNAs (Lee et al., 2015), binding the 7-methyl-guanosine (m7G) cap (Lamper et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2016) or through interactions with N-6-methyl-adenosine (m6A) post-transcriptional modifications in mRNAs (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2015 study.

claim: Binding of eIF3 to cis-regulatory elements in mRNA can lead to translation activation or repression, depending on the RNA sequence and structural context.
source: Binding to these cis-regulatory elements in mRNA can lead to translation activation or repression, depending on the RNA sequence and structural context (de la Parra et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2015; Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating context-dependent effects of eIF3 binding.

claim: Non-canonical functions of eIF3 can aid cell proliferation.
source: These non-canonical functions for eIF3 can aid cell proliferation (Lee et al., 2015), or allow cells to rapidly adapt to stresses such as heat shock (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Non-canonical functions of eIF3 allow cells to rapidly adapt to stresses such as heat shock.
source: These non-canonical functions for eIF3 can aid cell proliferation (Lee et al., 2015), or allow cells to rapidly adapt to stresses such as heat shock (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2015.

claim: T cell activation requires a rapid increase in protein synthesis within the first few hours that involves eIF3.
source: In the immune system, T cell activation requires a rapid increase in protein synthesis within the first few hours that also involves eIF3 (Ahern et al., 1974; Kleijn and Proud, 2002; Miyamoto et al., 2005; Ricciardi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on T cell activation and protein synthesis.

claim: Translation in non-activated lymphocytes is limited by the availability of translation initiation factors.
source: Translation in non-activated lymphocytes is limited by the availability of translation initiation factors (Ahern et al., 1974; Mao et al., 1992; Wolf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on translation regulation in lymphocytes.

claim: The mRNAs for several translation initiation factors, including those for many eIF3 subunits, are repressed in resting T cells and are rapidly translated within hours of activation.
source: The mRNAs for several translation initiation factors, including those for many eIF3 subunits, are repressed in resting T cells and are rapidly translated within hours of activation (Wolf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2020.

claim: Nearly inactive eIF3 in quiescent T cells is activated to form translation initiation complexes in the first few hours after stimulation.
source: Additionally, nearly inactive eIF3 in quiescent T cells is activated to form translation initiation complexes in the first few hours after stimulation (Miyamoto et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyamoto et al., 2005.

claim: Activation of eIF3 coincides with the recruitment of subunit eIF3j to eIF3 and translation initiation complexes.
source: Activation of eIF3 coincides with the recruitment of subunit eIF3j to eIF3 and translation initiation complexes (Miyamoto et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyamoto et al., 2005.

claim: Post-translational modifications contribute to the early increase in translation during T cell activation, for example activation of the guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B.
source: Post-translational modifications are also thought to contribute to the early increase in translation, for example activation of the guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B (Kleijn and Proud, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kleijn and Proud, 2002.

claim: The level of the canonical mRNA cap-binding complex eIF4F increases much later after T cell activation.
source: By contrast, the level of the canonical mRNA cap-binding complex eIF4F–composed of translation initiation factors eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF4A–increases much later after T cell activation (Mao et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mao et al., 1992.

claim: Translation of specific transcripts involved in glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis occurs within 1–3 days of T cell activation and depends on the activity of eIF4F.
source: Translation of these specific transcripts involved in glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis occurs within 1–3 days of T cell activation (Ricciardi et al., 2018), and depends on the activity of eIF4F.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ricciardi et al., 2018 and inference about eIF4F dependence.

claim: Hundreds of mRNAs translationally repressed in resting T cells are rapidly translated within hours after activation, including those encoding key transcription factors and ribosomal proteins.
source: Hundreds of other mRNAs translationally repressed in resting T cells are rapidly translated within hours after activation, including those encoding key transcription factors and ribosomal proteins, in addition to the translation initiation factors noted above (Wolf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2020.

claim: Most mRNAs rapidly translated after T cell activation are sensitive to mTOR inhibition.
source: Most of these mRNAs are sensitive to mTOR inhibition, highlighting the importance of eIF4F for the translation of these specific transcripts.
evidence: Based on inference from the role of mTOR in regulating eIF4F activity.

claim: A small subset of mRNAs evade mTOR inhibition by an unknown mechanism.
source: However, a small subset of mRNAs evade mTOR inhibition by an unknown mechanism (Wolf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2020.

claim: T cells are activated when a foreign antigen is recognized by the T cell receptor (TCR).
source: In the adaptive immune system, T cells are activated when a foreign antigen is recognized by the T cell receptor (TCR).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of T cell biology.

claim: Robust T cell activation requires a second signal generated by interactions between the T cell and antigen presenting cell mediated by the co-receptor CD28.
source: However, robust T cell activation requires a second signal generated by interactions between the T cell and antigen presenting cell mediated by the co-receptor CD28 (Esensten et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Esensten et al., 2016 and established immunological knowledge.

claim: The two-signal mechanism enables T cells to adopt a fully active state and avoid becoming unresponsive.
source: This two-signal mechanism enables T cells to adopt a fully active state and avoid becoming unresponsive (Chen and Flies, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Flies, 2013.

claim: T cell activation can be mimicked in vitro using antibodies targeting both the TCR and CD28 (anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies, respectively).
source: The process of T cell activation can be mimicked in vitro using antibodies targeting both the TCR and CD28 (anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies, respectively) (Harding et al., 1992), which has greatly aided the dissection of molecular mechanisms underlying T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harding et al., 1992.

claim: T cells can be engineered to express chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) that specifically target antigens on the surface of cancer cells.
source: T cells can be engineered to express chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) that specifically target antigens on the surface of cancer cells, and signal through protein elements derived from both the TCR and CD28 or other co-stimulatory receptors (Chen and Flies, 2013; Globerson Levin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Flies, 2013 and Globerson Levin et al., 2021.

claim: CAR T cells have been used to treat CD19-positive B cell malignancies with dramatic results.
source: The most successful of these CAR T cells have been used to treat CD19-positive B cell malignancies, with dramatic results (Friedman et al., 2018; Kalos et al., 2011; Kochenderfer et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: CAR T cells have drawbacks including toxicity to the patient, CAR T cell exhaustion, limited persistence and poor efficacy in solid tumors.
source: However, CAR T cells still have a number of drawbacks, including toxicity to the patient, CAR T cell exhaustion, limited persistence and poor efficacy in solid tumors.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CAR T cell limitations.

claim: In activated Jurkat cells, eIF3 crosslinked to RNA on eight of the 13 eIF3 subunits: EIF3A, EIF3B, EIF3D, EIF3G, EIF3C, EIF3E, EIF3F, and EIF3L.
source: In the Jurkat PAR-CLIP experiments, RNA crosslinked to eight of the 13 eIF3 subunits, as identified by mass spectrometry: subunits EIF3A, EIF3B, EIF3D, and EIF3G as previously seen in HEK293T cells (Lee et al., 2015), as well as subunits EIF3C, EIF3E, EIF3F, and EIF3L (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and PAR-CLIP results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: eIF3 crosslinked to a substantially larger number of mRNAs (~75 x more) in activated Jurkat cells compared to control non-activated cells.
source: Consistent with its role in T cell activation, eIF3 crosslinked to a substantially larger number of mRNAs (~75 x more) in activated Jurkat cells compared to control non-activated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1D and Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data comparing activated and non-activated cells.

claim: In activated Jurkat cells, eIF3 interacted with mRNAs enriched for those encoding proteins central to immune cell function.
source: Notably, in activated Jurkat cells eIF3 interacted with mRNAs enriched for those encoding proteins central to immune cell function, in contrast to those previously identified in HEK293T cells (Lee et al., 2015; Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The extent of eIF3 crosslinking in activated Jurkat cells does not correlate with mRNA abundance based on transcription profiling.
source: The extent of eIF3 crosslinking in activated Jurkat cells does not correlate with mRNA abundance based on transcription profiling carried out in parallel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison of PAR-CLIP data with transcriptome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The enrichment of immune system related mRNAs in eIF3 PAR-CLIP reflects the involvement of eIF3 in specific regulation of T cell activation.
source: This suggests the enrichment of immune system related mRNAs reflects the involvement of eIF3 in specific regulation of T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between eIF3 crosslinking and mRNA abundance.

claim: eIF3 showed a multitude of crosslinking patterns on different mRNAs in activated Jurkat cells.
source: In activated Jurkat cells, eIF3 showed a multitude of crosslinking patterns on different mRNAs (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, G and H), consistent with varied roles for eIF3 in T cell activation and function.
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data showing different crosslinking patterns in Figures 1D-E.

claim: Many mRNAs have a single PAR-CLIP site in the 5'-UTR as observed in HEK293T cells.
source: Many of the mRNAs have a single PAR-CLIP site in the 5'-UTR as observed in HEK293T cells (Lee et al., 2015; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data and comparison with previous HEK293T results.

claim: eIF3 crosslinked to some mRNAs across the entire length of the transcript, from the beginning of the 5'-UTR through the 3'-UTR ('pan-mRNA' pattern).
source: However, eIF3 crosslinked to some mRNAs across the entire length of the transcript, from the beginning of the 5'-UTR through the 3'-UTR (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The 'pan-mRNA' pattern of eIF3 crosslinking includes polyadenylated mRNAs as well as histone mRNAs.
source: This 'pan-mRNA' pattern of eIF3 crosslinking–which includes polyadenylated mRNAs as well as histone mRNAs–has not been observed before.
evidence: Based on analysis of PAR-CLIP data including histone mRNAs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: A number of pan-mRNAs encode proteins important for T cell activation, including both the alpha and beta subunits of the T cell receptor (TCR), subunits TCRA and TCRB.
source: Interestingly, a number of these mRNAs encode proteins important for T cell activation, including both the alpha and beta subunits of the T cell receptor (TCR), subunits TCRA and TCRB (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 1E and pathway analysis.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNAs did not co-localize with either P bodies or stress granules in Jurkat cells activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies.
source: Interestingly, the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs did not co-localize with either P bodies or stress granules, or with each other in Jurkat cells activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies, which induce both TCR and CD28 coreceptor signaling required for robust T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992; Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by FISH analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNAs are not translationally repressed but are possibly activated by eIF3 binding.
source: These results suggest that the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs are not translationally repressed but are possibly activated by eIF3 binding.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of colocalization with P bodies and stress granules.

claim: eIF3 only immunoprecipitated the pan-crosslinked mRNAs (TCRA, TCRB, DUSP2) from polysomes, but not mRNAs that only crosslinked to eIF3 through their 5'-UTRs (EGR1, TRIM28).
source: Using primers to the CDS regions of the mRNAs, we found that eIF3 only immunoprecipitated the pan-crosslinked mRNAs (TCRA, TCRB, DUSP2) from polysomes, but not mRNAs that only crosslinked to eIF3 through their 5'-UTRs (EGR1, TRIM28) (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: All tested mRNAs (TCRA, TCRB, DUSP2, EGR1, TRIM28) are present in translating ribosomes and can be immunoprecipitated with eIF3 when the mRNAs are left intact.
source: Importantly, all these mRNAs are present in translating ribosomes and can be immunoprecipitated with eIF3 when the mRNAs are left intact (RNase H treatment without DNA oligos) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In activated T cells, eIF3 remains bound to the coding sequences (CDS) of the pan-mRNAs TCRA, TCRB, and DUSP2 in polysomes independent of their 5'-UTR and 3'-UTR elements.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that, in activated T cells, eIF3 remains bound to the coding sequences (CDS) of the pan-mRNAs TCRA, TCRB, and DUSP2 in polysomes independent of their 5'-UTR and 3'-UTR elements.
evidence: Inferred from the RNase H digestion experiments showing eIF3 binding to CDS after UTR removal.

claim: The pan-mRNA crosslinking pattern of TCRA and TCRB mRNAs reflects eIF3 binding to these mRNAs during translation elongation.
source: These results further support the model that the pan-mRNA crosslinking pattern of TCRA and TCRB mRNAs reflects eIF3 binding to these mRNAs during translation elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the polysome analysis showing eIF3 remains bound to CDS during translation.

claim: T cells expressing the reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR sequences produced substantially higher luminescence that peaked 1 hr after activation.
source: T cells expressing the reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR sequences produced substantially higher luminescence that peaked 1 hr after activation, while cells expressing nanoluciferase from reporters with a deletion or reversal of the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site sequence showed no apparent burst in translation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cells expressing nanoluciferase from reporters with a deletion or reversal of the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site sequence showed no apparent burst in translation.
source: T cells expressing the reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR sequences produced substantially higher luminescence that peaked 1 hr after activation, while cells expressing nanoluciferase from reporters with a deletion or reversal of the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site sequence showed no apparent burst in translation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The TCRA ΔPAR or R*PAR or TCRB ΔPAR or R*PAR mutations did not cause significant defects in the nanoluciferase mRNA levels when compared to reporters with the corresponding WT 3'-UTR sequences.
source: The TCRA ΔPAR or R*PAR or TCRB ΔPAR or R*PAR mutations, however, did not cause significant defects in the nanoluciferase mRNA levels when compared to reporters with the corresponding WT 3'-UTR sequences (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The burst in nanoluciferase expression observed with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR sequences is regulated posttranscriptionally.
source: This suggests the burst in nanoluciferase expression observed with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR sequences is regulated posttranscriptionally.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutations do not affect mRNA levels but do affect protein expression.

claim: Less nanoluciferase mRNA bound to eIF3 when the 3'-UTR PAR-CLIP site was either deleted or reversed, compared to nanoluciferase mRNAs carrying the WT TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR.
source: Immunoprecipitation of eIF3 followed by qRT-PCR quantification of nanoluciferase mRNA showed that less nanoluciferase mRNA bound to eIF3 when the 3'-UTR PAR-CLIP site was either deleted or reversed, compared to nanoluciferase mRNAs carrying the WT TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements that crosslinked to eIF3 do not share any conserved sequences or RNA structural elements.
source: Interestingly, although the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements that crosslinked to eIF3 do not share any conserved sequences or RNA structural elements (Xu and Mathews, 2016), the above results support the idea that eIF3 binding to specific sequences or structures within the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs controls a burst in translation after T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Mathews, 2016 for RNA structure analysis.

claim: eIF3 binding to specific sequences or structures within the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs controls a burst in translation after T cell activation.
source: Interestingly, although the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements that crosslinked to eIF3 do not share any conserved sequences or RNA structural elements (Xu and Mathews, 2016), the above results support the idea that eIF3 binding to specific sequences or structures within the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs controls a burst in translation after T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the reporter experiments showing 3'-UTR-dependent translation burst.

claim: The HCV IRES IIIabc and JUN sequences increased nanoluciferase translation when replacing the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site in the TCRA 3'-UTR.
source: By contrast to the TCRA ΔPAR 3'-UTR, the HCV IRES IIIabc and JUN sequences increased nanoluciferase translation (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The HCV IRES IIIabc and JUN sequences rescued eIF3 binding to the reporter mRNAs upon T cell activation.
source: The HCV IRES IIIabc and JUN sequences also rescued eIF3 binding to the reporter mRNAs (Figure 3I) upon T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The engineered 3'-UTRs recruit eIF3 to the mRNA.
source: These results are consistent with the engineered 3'-UTRs recruiting eIF3 to the mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of eIF3 binding and translation by HCV IRES and JUN sequences.

claim: The dynamics of translation activation induced by the 3'-UTRs harboring the HCV IRES or JUN sequences did not recapitulate the effects of the WT TCRA 3'-UTR.
source: However, the dynamics of translation activation induced by the 3'-UTRs harboring the HCV IRES or JUN sequences did not recapitulate the effects of the WT TCRA 3'-UTR.
evidence: Supported by comparison of luciferase kinetics in Figure 3G.

claim: Both engineered 3'-UTRs (HCV IRES and JUN) increased nanoluciferase levels within 30 min of activation, in contrast to the WT TCRA 3'-UTR.
source: Both engineered 3'-UTRs increased nanoluciferase levels within 30 min of activation, in contrast to the WT TCRA 3'-UTR (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Neither engineered 3'-UTR led to a marked decrease of nanoluciferase levels after the 1 hr peak in luminescence seen with the WT TCRA 3'-UTR.
source: Furthermore, neither engineered 3'-UTR led to a marked decrease of nanoluciferase levels after the 1 hr peak in luminescence seen with the WT TCRA 3'-UTR (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs are necessary and sufficient to drive a burst in translation after T cell activation.
source: Taken together, the nanoluciferase reporter experiments reveal the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs are necessary and sufficient to drive a burst in translation after T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the reporter experiments showing 3'-UTR-dependent translation burst.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements recruit eIF3 to the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs to drive a burst in translation of the TCR alpha and beta subunits.
source: They also suggest these 3'-UTR elements recruit eIF3 to the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs to drive a burst in translation of the TCR alpha and beta subunits.
evidence: Inferred from the reporter experiments and eIF3 binding data.

claim: Anti-CD28 stimulation alone was sufficient to cause a transient burst in translation in the nanoluciferase reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs.
source: We found anti-CD28 stimulation alone was sufficient to cause a transient burst in translation in the nanoluciferase reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs, whereas anti-CD3 stimulation caused a continuous increase in reporter protein expression (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Anti-CD3 stimulation caused a continuous increase in reporter protein expression.
source: We found anti-CD28 stimulation alone was sufficient to cause a transient burst in translation in the nanoluciferase reporters with the WT TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs, whereas anti-CD3 stimulation caused a continuous increase in reporter protein expression (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The burst in translation required the reporters to be membrane tethered via a N-terminal transmembrane helix (from CD3zeta) that is co-translationally inserted into the membrane.
source: Interestingly, the burst in translation required the reporters to be membrane tethered via a N-terminal transmembrane helix (from CD3zeta) that is co-translationally inserted into the membrane (Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005; Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–1C), consistent with the fact that CD28 signaling involves multiple membrane-associated events (Boomer and Green, 2010).
evidence: Supported by comparison of membrane-tethered and non-tethered reporters in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reporters with TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR 3'-UTRs failed to show a burst in expression even when the reporter proteins were tethered to the membrane.
source: Moreover, the reporters with TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR 3'-UTRs failed to show a burst in expression even when the reporter proteins were tethered to the membrane (Figure 4A–D), supporting the role for eIF3 in the translational burst.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The CD28 costimulatory pathway drives an early burst in TCR translation after T cell activation, mediated by eIF3 binding to the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs.
source: Taken together, these results support the model that the CD28 costimulatory pathway drives an early burst in TCR translation after T cell activation, mediated by eIF3 binding to the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs.
evidence: Inferred from the CD28-dependent translation burst experiments.

claim: Treatment with the mTOR inhibitor Torin 1 had no effect on the rapid increase in reporter expression.
source: In T cells expressing the membrane-tethered nanoluciferase reporter mRNA with the WT TCRA 3'-UTR (Figure 4A), treatment with the mTOR inhibitor Torin 1 had no effect on the rapid increase in reporter expression as seen with the DMSO control.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data with mTOR inhibitor shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The burst in nanoluciferase expression was blocked when AKT kinase activity was inhibited with AZD5363 (AZD).
source: However, the burst in nanoluciferase expression was blocked when AKT kinase activity was inhibited with AZD5363 (AZD) (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–1E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data with AKT inhibitor shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The transient burst in TCR expression likely requires specific interactions between eIF3 and the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs and also membrane-proximal CD28 signaling.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the transient burst in TCR expression likely requires specific interactions between eIF3 and the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs and also membrane-proximal CD28 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of 3'-UTR dependence, CD28 dependence, and membrane tethering requirement.

claim: T cell activation requires CD28 costimulation to elicit an initial positive signal involving AKT kinase activity, which is later repressed by a negative feedback loop also mediated by CD28 signaling and cis-regulatory elements in the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs.
source: Furthermore, these results support a model in which T cell activation requires CD28 costimulation to elicit an initial positive signal involving AKT kinase activity, which is later repressed by a negative feedback loop also mediated by CD28 signaling and cis-regulatory elements in the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs.
evidence: Inferred from the kinetics of the translation burst and AKT dependence.

claim: TCRA levels rose and peaked approximately one hour after T cell activation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies.
source: As seen with the nanoluciferase reporters, TCRA levels rose and peaked approximately one hour after T cell activation with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The early burst in TCRA translation is dependent on CD28 but not on TCR signaling.
source: Furthermore, the early burst in TCRA translation is dependent on CD28 but not on TCR signaling (Figure 5A), also as observed with membrane-tethered reporters (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A comparing different activation conditions.

claim: PCR analysis showed successful deletion of the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site in the TCRA 3'-UTR or in the TCRB 3'-UTR (TCRA ΔPAR or TCRB ΔPAR, respectively) in 43–49% of the alleles.
source: PCR analysis showed successful deletion of the eIF3 PAR-CLIP site in the TCRA 3'-UTR or in the TCRB 3'-UTR (TCRA ΔPAR or TCRB ΔPAR, respectively) in 43–49% of the alleles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by PCR analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SC control cells exhibited a substantial burst in TCRA protein levels immediately after activation (~1 hr).
source: The SC control cells – which should behave as wild-type T cells – exhibited a substantial burst in TCRA protein levels immediately after activation (~1 hr).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TCRA protein levels were nearly absent or clearly reduced at early time points after activation in both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cell populations.
source: By contrast, TCRA protein levels were nearly absent or clearly reduced at early time points after activation in both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cell populations (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells had fewer cells forming TCR clusters, especially at the early time point compared to SC control cells when activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28.
source: Both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells had fewer cells forming TCR clusters, especially at the early time point compared to SC control cells when activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells expressed lower amounts of cell surface TCR compared to SC control cells or cells edited with a single gRNA when tested by flow cytometric analysis after PMA + I activation.
source: Consistent with the TCRA expression levels observed in western blots and the rate of TCR clustering (Figure 5B and C), both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells expressed lower amounts of cell surface TCR compared to SC control cells or cells edited with a single gRNA when tested by flow cytometric analysis after PMA + I activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Fewer cells in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR CD8+ and CD4+ primary T cell populations expressed CD69 at early time points after activation (5–8 hr).
source: Fewer cells in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR CD8+ and CD4+ primary T cell populations expressed CD69 at early time points after activation (5–8 hr) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B) and fewer expressed both CD69 and CD25 at later time points after activation, compared to SC control cells (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Fewer cells in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR populations expressed both CD69 and CD25 at later time points after activation, compared to SC control cells.
source: Fewer cells in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR CD8+ and CD4+ primary T cell populations expressed CD69 at early time points after activation (5–8 hr) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B) and fewer expressed both CD69 and CD25 at later time points after activation, compared to SC control cells (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR T cell populations secreted lower amounts of the stimulatory cytokines IL2 and IFNγ, compared to the SC control cells.
source: We also found the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR T cell populations secreted lower amounts of the stimulatory cytokines IL2 (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 4E) and IFNγ (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4F), compared to the SC control cells.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: The TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR primary T cell populations exhibited multiple early and late T cell activation defects.
source: Taken together, the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR primary T cell populations exhibited multiple early and late T cell activation defects.
evidence: Inferred from the combined defects in TCR clustering, CD69/CD25 expression, and cytokine secretion.

claim: After T cell activation, eIF3 binding to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs drives an early burst in TCR translation that is required for many subsequent steps in T cell activation.
source: These results support the model that after T cell activation, eIF3 binding to the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs drives an early burst in TCR translation that is required for many subsequent steps in T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing 3'-UTR-dependent TCR translation burst and downstream activation defects.

claim: WT Jurkat cells showed a TCR translational burst that peaked 5–8 hr after activation.
source: WT Jurkat cells showed a TCR translational burst that peaked 5–8 hr after activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR Jurkat cell populations expressed lower levels of the TCR proteins compared to WT cells, and failed to show a burst in TCR expression at early time points after activation.
source: By contrast, both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR Jurkat cell populations expressed lower levels of the TCR proteins compared to WT cells, and failed to show a burst in TCR expression at early time points after activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: TCRA and TCRB mRNA levels were unaffected or even increased in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR Jurkat cells.
source: Importantly, TCRA and TCRB mRNA levels were unaffected or even increased in the TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR Jurkat cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B and C), similar to our observations with nanoluciferase reporters in primary T cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B and C.

claim: TCR expression levels are regulated post-transcriptionally by eIF3 interactions with the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements.
source: This is consistent with TCR expression levels being regulated post-transcriptionally by eIF3 interactions with the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mRNA levels are unchanged but protein levels are reduced in ΔPAR cells.

claim: In both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells, eIF3 bound to significantly lower amounts of the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs compared to WT cells at both the 5 hr and 8 hr time points after anti-CD3/anti-CD28 activation.
source: In both TCRA ΔPAR and TCRB ΔPAR cells, eIF3 bound to significantly lower amounts of the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs compared to WT cells at both the 5 hr and 8 hr time points after anti-CD3/anti-CD28 activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5D and E.

claim: Deleting the eIF3 PAR-CLIP sites in the 3'-UTR disrupts eIF3 interactions with the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs substantially.
source: This indicates deleting the eIF3 PAR-CLIP sites in the 3'-UTR disrupts eIF3 interactions with the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs substantially.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced eIF3 binding to TCRA and TCRB mRNAs in ΔPAR cells.

claim: eIF3 binding to the 3'-UTR elements of the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs mediates the rapid burst in TCR translation after T cell activation.
source: Together with the nanoluciferase reporter experiments in primary T cells (Figure 3), these results support the model that eIF3 binding to the 3'-UTR elements of the TCRA and TCRB mRNAs mediates the rapid burst in TCR translation after T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of reporter experiments and endogenous TCR analysis.

claim: The WPRE and 3'-LTR 3'-UTR elements failed to induce the early burst in nanoluciferase expression.
source: In contrast to the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs (Figures 3 and 4), the WPRE and 3'-LTR 3'-UTR elements failed to induce the early burst in nanoluciferase expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fusing the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR sequences to engineered CAR open reading frames could be used to obtain more physiological expression dynamics seen for the endogenous TCR.
source: These data suggest that fusing the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR sequences to engineered CAR open reading frames could be used to obtain more physiological expression dynamics seen for the endogenous TCR.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of TCRA/TCRB 3'-UTRs with WPRE and 3'-LTR.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs induced a burst in anti-CD19 CAR protein levels within 5 hr of NALM6 cell addition, whereas the WPRE and 3'-LTR sequences delayed the burst in CAR expression to ~24 hr.
source: Interestingly, the TCRA and TCRB 3'-UTRs induced a burst in anti-CD19 CAR protein levels within 5 hr of NALM6 cell addition, whereas the WPRE and 3'-LTR sequences delayed the burst in CAR expression to ~24 hr (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CAR T cells expressing the CAR using either the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR showed more robust killing of two tumor cell lines compared to CARs using either the WPRE or 3'-LTR 3'-UTRs.
source: Using in vitro cytotoxicity assays (Figure 6E), CAR T cells expressing the CAR using either the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR showed more robust killing of two tumor cell lines compared to CARs using either the WPRE or 3'-LTR 3'-UTRs.
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: CAR T cells expressing the CAR using either the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR generally propagated more robustly in the presence of the target tumor cells regardless of condition.
source: Interestingly, CAR T cells expressing the CAR using either the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR generally propagated more robustly in the presence of the target tumor cells regardless of condition (Figure 6F–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–1D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by CAR T cell counts in cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 6F-G and supplements.

claim: The results are consistent with the importance of an early burst of CAR translation for optimal CAR T cell function.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with the importance of an early burst of CAR translation for optimal CAR T cell function.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between early CAR expression burst and improved killing.

claim: Using the native TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs for CAR expression can be used to improve CAR T cell function.
source: These results also support the idea that using the native TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs for CAR expression can be used to improve CAR T cell function.
evidence: Inferred from the improved killing and propagation of CAR T cells using TCRA/TCRB 3'-UTRs.

claim: The patterns of eIF3 crosslinking suggest an active role for eIF3 in promoting translation of immune-related mRNAs.
source: Interestingly, the patterns of eIF3 crosslinking, which for a number of mRNAs include interactions with the protein coding sequence and 3'-UTR (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H), suggest an active role for eIF3 in promoting translation of these mRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the pan-mRNA crosslinking pattern observed in PAR-CLIP data.

claim: The two examples of pan-mRNAs examined (TCRA and TCRB) do not colocalize with P bodies or stress granules.
source: In support of this model, the two examples of pan-mRNAs we examined here (TCRA and TCRB) do not colocalize with P bodies or stress granules (Figure 1F) and binding to eIF3 includes the mRNA coding sequence on translating ribosomes (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH and polysome analysis data.

claim: This eIF3-mediated translation activation is transient, lasting only 1–2 hr in primary T cells.
source: However, this eIF3-mediated translation activation is transient, lasting only 1–2 hr in primary T cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing transient TCRA expression burst.

claim: The TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements are necessary and sufficient to control the burst in translation after T cell activation.
source: Importantly, the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements are necessary and sufficient to control this burst in translation (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by reporter experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: eIF3 can remain associated with translating ribosomes.
source: Recent evidence suggests that eIF3 can remain associated with translating ribosomes (Bohlen et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2020), a phenomenon that seems to be enhanced for the pan-mRNAs identified here.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on eIF3 association with ribosomes.

claim: It is possible that the 5'-UTRs and 3'-UTRs of some mRNAs are in close proximity on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum, and eIF3 binding to the 3'-UTR could directly influence the efficiency of translation initiation from the 5'-UTR.
source: It is possible that the 5'-UTRs and 3'-UTRs of some mRNAs are in close proximity, that is on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (Christensen et al., 1987; Christensen and Bourne, 1999), and eIF3 binding to the 3'-UTR could directly influence the efficiency of translation initiation from the 5'-UTR.
evidence: Speculative model based on known mRNA circularization and ER localization.

claim: T cells must cross a threshold of T cell receptor signaling to commit to activation and proliferation.
source: Recent experiments indicate that T cells must cross a threshold of T cell receptor signaling to commit to activation and proliferation (Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Au-Yeung et al., 2014), setting up a 'digital' response to antigen recognition (Allison et al., 2016; Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Au-Yeung et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on TCR signaling thresholds.

claim: The response threshold involves integration of intensity and duration of TCR signaling.
source: The response threshold involves integration of intensity and duration of TCR signaling (Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Au-Yeung et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2018), and spans a wide range of TCR antigen affinity (Allison et al., 2016; Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Au-Yeung et al., 2014; Richard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on TCR signaling dynamics.

claim: T cell commitment to clonal expansion and differentiation can occur within as little as 1–2 hr of TCR stimulation for effector CD4+ and naive CD8+ T cells.
source: Notably, T cell commitment to clonal expansion and differentiation can occur within as little as 1–2 hr of TCR stimulation for effector CD4+ and naive CD8+ T cells (Iezzi et al., 1998; van Stipdonk et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on T cell commitment timing.

claim: The time period of 1-2 hours spans the burst in TCR protein synthesis mediated by eIF3 interactions with the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements.
source: Remarkably, this time period spans the burst in TCR protein synthesis mediated by eIF3 interactions with the TCRA and TCRB mRNA 3'-UTR elements (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between TCR burst timing and T cell commitment timing.

claim: Naive CD4+ T cells require a longer duration of TCR signaling of ~20 hr.
source: Naive CD4+ T cells require a longer duration of TCR signaling of ~20 hr (Iezzi et al., 1998; Schrum et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on naive CD4+ T cell activation.

claim: The burst in TCRA translation in the first 1–2 hr of stimulation correlates with multiple downstream events required for T cell activation and function.
source: Our observation of the burst in TCRA translation (and by implication TCRB translation) (Koning et al., 1988; Ohashi et al., 1985) in the first 1–2 hr of stimulation also correlates with multiple downstream events required for T cell activation and function.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between TCR burst and downstream activation events.

claim: Loss of the burst in TCR protein synthesis delayed formation of TCR clusters.
source: For example, loss of the burst in TCR protein synthesis delayed formation of TCR clusters (Figure 5C), suggesting that surface expression of the TCR (Cochran et al., 2001; Huppa and Davis, 2003) is also impacted by the dynamics of TCRA and TCRB translation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced TCR clustering in ΔPAR cells.

claim: Subsequent events in T cell activation including CD69 and CD25 expression, and IL2 and IFNγ secretion, were equally affected in CD8+ and CD4+ cells in which the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR PAR-CLIP sites were deleted.
source: Although we were not able to distinguish levels of TCR translation in isolated CD8+ and CD4+ T cells (Figure 5), subsequent events in T cell activation including CD69 and CD25 expression, and IL2 and IFNγ secretion, were equally affected in CD8+ and CD4+ cells in which the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTR PAR-CLIP sites were deleted (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and ELISA data shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: CD28 engagement serves as the second signal required for T cell activation and affects the first minutes of TCR-mediated signaling.
source: In an immune response, CD28 engagement serves as the second signal required for T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992; Harding and Allison, 1993) and affects the first minutes of TCR-mediated signaling (Green et al., 2000; Green et al., 1994; Michel et al., 2001; Shahinian et al., 1993; Tuosto and Acuto, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on CD28 costimulation.

claim: CD28-mediated signaling is needed for the burst of TCR translation on the hour timescale in primary T cells.
source: Here, we show CD28-mediated signaling is also needed for the burst of TCR translation on the hour timescale in primary T cells (Buckler et al., 2006; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by reporter experiments showing CD28-dependent translation burst.

claim: eIF3 controls TCRA and TCRB mRNA translation during the first critical hours after antigen recognition that leads to subsequent T cell commitment to proliferation and differentiation.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that eIF3 controls TCRA and TCRB mRNA translation during the first critical hours after antigen recognition that leads to subsequent T cell commitment to proliferation and differentiation (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing eIF3-dependent TCR translation burst and its effects on T cell activation.

claim: The CD28-dependent burst in TCR translation requires cotranslational membrane targeting.
source: We found the CD28-dependent burst in TCR translation requires cotranslational membrane targeting, consistent with the fact that CD28-mediated signaling occurs at the plasma membrane (Boomer and Green, 2010) and the fact that both the TCRA and TCRB subunits are integral membrane proteins.
evidence: Supported by experiments with membrane-tethered reporters.

claim: Additional immune-related mRNAs in the PAR-CLIP experiment encode membrane proteins or secreted proteins which may be particularly sensitive to CD28 signaling.
source: We also observed additional immune-related mRNAs in the PAR-CLIP experiment that encode membrane proteins or secreted proteins (i.e. B2M, CD28, CD3D, HLA-E, and LAT in Supplementary file 5, and TAP1 and TAP2 in Supplementary file 3) which may be particularly sensitive to CD28 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the PAR-CLIP data and the membrane-targeting requirement for the translation burst.

claim: The requirement for CD28 in PD-1 mediated inhibition of T cell activation suggests eIF3-mediated control of TCR expression may affect PD-1 checkpoint blockade-based cancer immunotherapy.
source: The requirement for CD28 in PD-1 mediated inhibition of T cell activation (Hui et al., 2017; Kamphorst et al., 2017) also suggests eIF3-mediated control of TCR expression may affect PD-1 checkpoint blockade-based cancer immunotherapy (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative connection based on the role of CD28 in both TCR translation and PD-1 inhibition.

claim: AKT influences the rapid rise in translation during the TCR translation burst.
source: We found that AKT influences the rapid rise in translation (Figure 4E–F), but other kinases such as Tec-kinases (Andreotti et al., 2018; Gallagher et al., 2021; Hallumi et al., 2021) could also impact the translation burst.
evidence: Supported by AKT inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Using the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs dramatically shortened the lag time before the burst in CAR protein expression upon exposure to tumor cells.
source: With a clinically validated anti-CD19 CAR, we found that using the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs dramatically shortened the lag time before the burst in CAR protein expression upon exposure to tumor cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing earlier CAR expression with TCRA/TCRB 3'-UTRs.

claim: The short lag time in CAR expression correlated with improved tumor cell killing in cytotoxicity assays.
source: This short lag time correlated with improved tumor cell killing in cytotoxicity assays (Figure 6F and G, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing improved killing with TCRA/TCRB 3'-UTRs.

claim: Using the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs for CAR expression improved CAR T cell propagation in the presence of target tumor cells.
source: Interestingly, using the TCRA or TCRB mRNA 3'-UTRs for CAR expression also improved CAR T cell propagation in the presence of target tumor cells (Figure 6F and G, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: Supported by CAR T cell counts in cytotoxicity assays.

claim: CARs generally have a weaker affinity for their target ligand compared to TCRs for antigens presented on the cell surface.
source: For example, CARs generally have a weaker affinity for their target ligand compared to TCRs for antigens presented on the cell surface (Watanabe et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2018.

claim: CARs do not elicit immune synapses as observed for TCRs.
source: Furthermore, CARs do not elicit immune synapses as observed for TCRs (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2020.

claim: The burst in CAR protein expression using the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs was still not as rapid as that of the endogenous TCR in T cells stimulated by anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies.
source: Here, we observed the burst in CAR protein expression using the TCRA or TCRB 3'-UTRs was still not as rapid as that of the endogenous TCR in T cells stimulated by anti-CD3/anti-CD28 antibodies (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CAR and endogenous TCR expression kinetics.
